knitr::opts_chunk$set(collapse = TRUE, comment = "#>", fig.width = 7, fig.height = 4.5)

A scorecard records what each batter did. It does not say how much each
result was worth. A two-out single with the bases empty and a bases-loaded
single both count as one hit, but the second changes the game far more. This
vignette walks through five real scorecards, from batting lines to
situational run value, called RE24, and then places a scored game inside its
team's full season.

```{r setup}
library(daimondstats)
```

## 1. Reviewed scorecard plays

`reviewed_scorecards` holds 179 plate appearances read from five handwritten
team scorecards by the dAImond Inning app and then reviewed against MLB game
records. Each card covers one team's side of one game.

```{r}
d <- reviewed_scorecards
table(d$team)
head(d[c("game_id", "player", "inning", "play")])
```

Batting statistics come straight from these plays. Team rates pool counts
across players rather than averaging player rates.

```{r}
batting <- calculate_batting_stats(d)
counts <- c("PA", "AB", "H", "BB", "HBP", "SF", "TB")
team <- aggregate(batting[counts], batting["team"], sum)
team$OBP <- with(team, (H + BB + HBP) / (AB + BB + HBP + SF))
team$SLG <- with(team, TB / AB)
team[c("team", "PA", "H", "BB", "OBP", "SLG")]
```

## 2. Adding the base-out state

A scorecard reader sees the result of each plate appearance, not where the
runners stood. `reviewed_base_out` adds that context from MLB play-by-play
records: outs and occupied bases before and after each event, and runs scored
on it. Base masks add 1 for first, 2 for second and 4 for third, so 5 means
runners on first and third.

The 179 batting events join one to one with the scorecard plays by game and
event ID. Nine more rows are steals, wild pitches, a passed ball and a pickoff,
which are credited to the runner.

```{r}
b <- reviewed_base_out
joined <- merge(d, b[b$batting_event, ], by = c("game_id", "event_id"))
nrow(joined)
table(b$event_type[!b$batting_event])
```

## 3. Run expectancy and RE24

A run expectancy matrix gives the average runs scored from each of the 24
base-out states to the end of the inning. The package includes the published
FanGraphs matrix for a run environment of 4.15 runs per game.

```{r}
xtabs(expected_runs ~ bases + outs, run_expectancy_fangraphs)
```

RE24 for an event is the runs scored on it plus the expectancy after it, minus
the expectancy before it. `calculate_run_impact()` applies the matrix and
rejects any row not marked as verified.

```{r}
impact <- calculate_run_impact(b, run_expectancy_fangraphs)
impact[impact$game_id == "825071" & impact$inning == 4,
       c("player", "event_type", "outs_before", "bases_before",
         "outs_after", "bases_after", "runs_scored", "re24")]
```

A useful check: every inning starts with the bases empty and no outs (0.461
expected runs) and ends with three outs (zero), so a team's RE24 for a game is
its runs minus 0.461 for each inning it batted.

```{r}
aggregate(cbind(runs_scored, re24) ~ team, impact, sum)
```

## 4. Who added the most

`plot_run_impact()` totals RE24 by player and draws the largest totals.

```{r}
top <- plot_run_impact(impact, top = 12,
                       main = "RE24 by player, five reviewed scorecards")
head(top)
```

The ranking can differ from batting average. A player with one hit can rank
above a player with two if that hit came with runners on.

## 5. How unusual was the game you scored?

`reviewed_team_seasons` holds the full 162-game regular season for each
scorecard team, built from MLB schedules with `season_games()`.
`compare_personal_season()` places the games someone scored inside that
season. By default it matches home and away games, so a collection of mostly
home games is compared with other mostly-home collections.

The Twins scorecard is from a 3-2 road win over the White Sox. Against the
other road games of the 2024 Twins season, that one-run margin sits near the
middle:

```{r}
twins <- subset(reviewed_team_seasons, team == "Minnesota Twins")
set.seed(457)
one <- compare_personal_season(twins, "746804", metric = "run_diff")
one$summary[c("personal_mean", "season_mean", "reference_low",
              "reference_high", "reference_percentile")]
```

The same call works for a larger collection. Suppose a fan scored every Twins
home game in April 2024:

```{r}
april <- subset(twins, home & format(game_date, "%Y-%m") == "2024-04")
set.seed(457)
many <- compare_personal_season(twins, april$game_id)
many$summary[c("selected_games", "personal_mean", "season_mean",
               "reference_low", "reference_high", "reference_percentile")]
hist(many$simulated_means, breaks = 20, col = "#C6CBD2", border = "white",
     main = "Win rate of 12-game samples matched on home/away",
     xlab = "Winning percentage")
abline(v = many$summary$personal_mean, col = "#2864B4", lwd = 2)
```

The vertical line is the scored collection. If it sits well inside the
histogram, those games were typical of the season.

## Limits

- Five scorecards from different teams and seasons are a demonstration of
  the method, not a personal season. Totals over three to five plate appearances are noisy.
- One published matrix is applied to every game. Real run environments vary
  by season and park.
- RE24 measures what happened in context. It is not a prediction and does not
  show clutch ability.
- Base-out states come from MLB records, not from the scorecard reader. For
  scorecards of games without MLB records, runner positions would have to be
  entered or checked by hand before `calculate_run_impact()` can be used.

## Reference

Weinberg, Neil. 2014. "RE24." FanGraphs, July 30.
<https://library.fangraphs.com/misc/re24/>.
